text: Chapter One – Drip Feed Trials always seemed to start the same: sharp inhale, tug behind the ribs, then boots on asphalt and the hum of the Fog fading off. Dwight blinked against the gray light of the Bedham Preschool domain. The air already felt heavier here, like the whole world had exhaled but never breathed back in. The Fog deposited them separately, the way it sometimes did — Dwight materializing at the far end of the street, David a half-block down and already scanning the sightlines before he'd fully arrived. They found each other without incident. A quick glance around told them they were alone at the moment; the others having been dropped in somewhere else. That was fine. Normal. Survivors rarely arrived as a full set, and Badham's twisted little playground was familiar enough not to panic about. The preschool sat low against the grey sky, its painted murals faded to suggestions of color, the chain-link fence around the yard sagging in places where rust had won the argument with the metal. Neither of them had pulled Bedham in a while, the Entity seeming to favor the woodsier domains as of late for some reason. Dwight tried to remember if there was anything particular about the layout worth flagging and came up mostly empty. Standard build. Tight interior. The basement generator was the move — killers avoided it because the pipe hallway that divided the lower level into two rooms was a nightmare to navigate, all jutting valves and blind corners, and there were two ways up instead of one. It was the kind of start that let you bank some early progress before things went sideways, turning chases into slow collisions and smug laughter. You could get a gen nearly done before they even thought about trying. It was the easiest way to relax before the real chases started. Get your bearings, work out the rust from joints. So long as the killer wasn’t one of the teleporting ones, it should be easy enough. David seemed to be running the same thought, as he sized up the immediate area, took one look at the weathered shell of the preschool and sighed, squaring his shoulders. “Boiler room?” “Boiler room,” Dwight echoed. They crossed the threshold into the school, ducking under a rusted EXIT sign that had long since given up. Bedham never had doors — none of the buildings seemed to — just openings where the idea of a door had been removed, neat rectangles cut through plaster and expectation. Dwight had stopped finding it strange years ago — the absence of doors was just part of the grammar of this place, the particular way the Entity assembled things from memory and suggestion rather than reality. The hall beyond breathed dust. Paper curls clung to a corkboard with sun-bleached pushpins. A child’s drawing of a house had flaked down to a white outline of someplace else. Light pooled in thin yellow lines through warped blinds, and dust swirled lazily in the shafts like it was still caught mid-class. A noise from deeper in — something heavy scraping tile; a crash of furniture meeting wall — made both of them drop without thinking, pressing back against the hallway lockers. A second sound followed, wood on metal, unnecessary and dramatic. David angled Dwight behind him on reflex, only to freeze when the source revealed itself down the far corridor: Ghostface, draped in black and carelessly visible, filming his own vandalism as if bored by the lack of applause. He shoved a locker door until it bounced back, then flicked his phone toward it like he was rating the performance. He wasn't stalking. He wasn't even paying attention to the building around him, which was the only reason he hadn't already seen them. He was filming himself on his phone with one hand and picking up a small plastic chair with the other, examining it with the critical eye of someone who had found something deeply disappointing. He turned it over once, seemed to find it lacking, and hurled it sideways into the wall with a hollow clatter that echoed the length of the building. “Just Ghostface,” he muttered with a small eyeroll, shaking his head lightly as the tension left his shoulders. “Looks like he’s in one of his moods.” Dwight nodded. The relief came with a small, wry exhale. A visible killer was a polite killer. Danny’s menace lived in the corners — no point wasting fear when he was being obvious. As long as he wasn’t looking their way, who cared? If the killer was already goofing around like this, he was clearly not in the mood to do a proper hunt. So long as everyone stayed out of his line of sight, they should be fine. Had he actually cared today, he would have been stealthed, and they might have missed him entirely. Danny moved on down the far corridor without once looking their way, already pointing his phone at something else. The faint sound of his own commentary floated back to them, too distant to make out. They gave it a moment before moving again. They took the opposite stairwell, easing down into the basement beneath flickering bulbs and rust-streaked walls. Dwight tried not to notice the way his shoulder brushed the wall with every step. It felt narrower than it should’ve, but that was just adrenaline. It had to be. It was a preschool, after all. Made for small bodies. It didn’t help that Danny's terror radius had a particular weight to it, a low crawling pressure that played tricks if you let it. Even on the other side of the building, it thrummed uncomfortably against his chest. That’s all this was, most likely. Just nerves. The generator waited at the far wall—half-skinned, half-sunk in a trap of its own piping.
